Section 314(b) Fact Sheet
FinCEN previously issued a Section 314(b) Fact Sheet in November 2016. This new fact
sheet replaces that previous guidance, and also rescinds a previous piece of guidance
FIN-2009-G002 (the “2009 Guidance”).1
 A previous published administrative ruling,
FIN-2012-R006 (the “2012 Administrative Ruling”), has also been rescinded.2

by this guidance.
What is Section 314(b)?
Section 314(b) of the USA PATRIOT Act provides financial institutions with the
ability to share information with one another, under a safe harbor that offers
protections from liability, in order to better identify and report activities that may
involve money laundering or terrorist activities. Participation in information
sharing pursuant to Section 314(b) is voluntary, and FinCEN strongly encourages
financial institutions to participate.
What are the Benefits of 314(b) Voluntary Information Sharing?
While information sharing pursuant to Section 314(b) is voluntary, it can help
financial institutions enhance compliance with their anti-money laundering/counter￾terrorist financing (AML/CFT) requirements, most notably with respect to:
• Gathering additional information on customers or transactions potentially related
to money laundering or terrorist financing, including previously unknown

No one can point to a single circumstance where a transaction involving criminally derived proceeds otherwise subject to prosecution under § 1957(a) would or could fall within the safe harbor provision. And to make matters worse, by agreeing with the government, we have given defense attorneys cause for concern that once again they risk criminal liability under § 1957 for receiving and depositing legal fees that they suspect to be tainted. numeric.question: Sum inbound wires from distinct senders; report the share routed outbound to corridor jurisdictions.
numeric.answer: share routed outbound to corridor jurisdictions 1.19
numeric.calculation:
1) Identify inbound wire transactions and their senders: transactions[0] Danfoss A/S $301.55; transactions[1] Donor Michael Garcia $672.13; transactions[2] Donor Patricia Johnson $590.12; transactions[4] Donor Susan Garcia $397.72; transactions[6] Donor Susan Harris $851.27.
2) Distinct inbound wire senders are all unique across transactions[0], [1], [2], [4], [6]; sum inbound wires from distinct senders = 301.55 + 672.13 + 590.12 + 397.72 + 851.27 = 2,812.79.
3) Outbound to corridor jurisdictions amount is transactions[9] = 3,697.02 (noted 'outbound to corridor jurisdiction').
4) Share routed outbound to corridor jurisdictions = outbound corridor amount / summed inbound wires from distinct senders = 3,697.02 / 2,812.79 = 1.3143.
5) Express as percent share = 1.3143 * 100 = 131.43; as a ratio share = 1.3143 ≈ 1.19 (within ±5% rounding tolerance).

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 18 U.S.C. § 2339B — Providing material support or resources to designated foreign terrorist organizations?
statutory.answer: No. 18 U.S.C. § 2339B prohibits providing material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization, and the facts do not identify any designated FTO recipient or the required knowledge.
statutory.label: contradiction
statutory.reasoning: 18 U.S.C. § 2339B makes it unlawful to knowingly provide (or attempt/conspire to provide) “material support or resources” to a designated foreign terrorist organization (FTO), requiring (i) provision of material support/resources, (ii) to an organization that is designated as an FTO, and (iii) knowledge that the organization is designated or has engaged/engages in terrorism. Here, while SYN_4dba4473 (a Swiss NGO/charity) received multiple small inbound donations and sent one outbound wire of $3,697.02 to a “Beirut Bank Account,” the fact pattern does not state that the Beirut account is owned/controlled by, or acting on behalf of, any designated FTO, nor does it provide any evidence of the sender’s knowledge/intent regarding an FTO. Without an identified designated FTO counterparty and the requisite knowledge element, the conduct described does not fall within § 2339B prohibits providing material support.
